method: Manual comparison of cleaned pilot source rows with species-specific records in a separate published-proteome compilation, then checking accessible articles. Numerical agreement is evidence for follow-up, not proof that a workbook row originated from a given study.

records.evidence: Both the source profile and article report 61.1% Kunitz-type and 31.0% three-finger toxin; the paper describes a pooled Kenya venom sample.
records.unresolved: The row-level citation is absent and the NP category has a conflicting definition/value in the candidate 2015 paper versus a later review. Do not treat this as a verified join or a confirmed natriuretic-peptide measurement.

label_review.concern: The 2017 review reports 2.9% as natriuretic peptide and cites Laustsen 2015. Direct inspection of Figure 2 (PDF page 50) and its legend (page 34) in Laustsen 2015 shows the same 2.9% NP represents non-protein components. This is a serious primary-versus-review label conflict. The workbook has no row-level citations; its value matches, but its direct provenance is unproven.
label_review.action: Preserve the raw value and recorded label, flag this profile/category for source reconciliation before model use, and do not interpret it as a confirmed quantified natriuretic peptide measurement.
label_review.reanalysis_note: Ainsworth et al. 2018 reanalyzed Petras et al. 2016 top-down MS data, not demonstrably the Laustsen 2015 sample. Their peptide identification does not establish the provenance or reclassification of the workbook 2.9% value.

newer_primary_study.finding: 0.04% natriuretic peptides in a pooled Tanzanian sample using relative tryptic peptide peak areas; distinct sample, not a correction of the original row.

label_review.correction: Earlier project notes incorrectly described the 2015 figure as reporting 2.5%. Visual inspection of the original figure confirms 2.9%.

records.evidence: Papua New Guinea location and multiple values match a separately compiled record and an independent later description of the Herrera dataset: 68.3% PLA2, 13.0% Kunitz, 8.9% SVMP and 4.2% 3FTx. The available original manuscript independently reports 68.3% PLA2 for the Papua New Guinea sample.
records.unresolved: Direct row-to-study mapping is absent in the workbook; the corroborating description is a later paper, and the accessible source does not establish a link to any pilot photograph.

records.evidence: Six shared family values in the separate compilation match the row; a later review attributes 49.7% SVMP and 19.8% SVSP to the candidate study.
records.unresolved: The original workbook gives location as unknown and does not cite the individual row; compare with the original paper and its sampling details before accepting this join.

records.evidence: The source row and accessible research article both report 63.8% three-finger toxins and 11.4% PLA2; the article describes an eastern Indian sample.
records.unresolved: The workbook records only India and has no explicit citation per row. Numerical agreement is not conclusive proof of this mapping.

records.evidence: Workbook transcriptomics row reports 74.64% SVMP; Pla et al. report 74.64% toxin-encoding gene expression for SVMP and approximately 7.56% PLA2. These agree with the row values 74.64 and 7.6, respectively.
records.unresolved: Probable but not proven match. The workbook says South Africa, whereas the candidate paper states the single venom-gland specimen was Tanzanian. The proteomics venom in that paper was sourced separately from South Africa. Do not silently change the original location.

records.evidence: Workbook measured-protein row reports 77.5% SVMP; Pla et al. report 77.5% SVMP for the venom proteome of adult D. typus. The paper describes South African-origin venom, matching the workbook location.
records.unresolved: Probable but not verified row-level citation: match the full quantitative figure and supplementary table. Source sample is not demonstrated to be the same snake as the Tanzanian gland sample or any pilot photo.

unresolved_examples.reason: No matching primary study established in this review.
The candidate Herrera Australia record has several differing family values, including PLA2. Do not assign without investigating the discrepancy.
